murine acquired immunodeficiency syndrome: involvement of Fas-Fas ligand interaction. Murine acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (MAIDS) is caused by a defective murine leukemia virus. The disease is characterized by abnormal lymphoproliferation, impaired T and B cell function and aberrant regulation of cytokines. Recent studies have shown that Fas-Fas ligand interaction plays a crucial role in the pathogenesis of MAIDS. Fas is a type I transmembrane receptor belonging to the tumor necrosis factor (TNF) receptor superfamily. It is expressed on the surface of various cells, including T and B lymphocytes, and serves as a critical mediator of apoptosis, or programmed cell death. Fas ligand (FasL), on the other hand, is a type II transmembrane protein that binds to Fas and initiates the apoptotic process. In MAIDS, the virus infects and destroys CD4+ T cells, leading to a profound T cell deficiency. However, the virus also infects and transforms macrophages, which then express high levels of FasL. This process involves resection of one strand of a broken end to produce a single stranded overhang that can invade the helix of the sister chromatid. Polymerase then uses the sister chromatid to fill in sequence on the broken ends and the strands are resolved to separate, complete sister chromatids \[[@R26], [@R31]\]. During the rest of the cell cycle, or in non-dividing cells, no identical sequence template is available to allow HDR to proceed, so the cell turns to the faster but more error prone process of Non-Homologous End Joining (NHEJ) \[[@R32], [@R33]\]. The sister chromatids serve as templates for Homology Dependent Repair (HDR) through the process of resection and synthesis. One strand of a broken end is resected to create a single-stranded overhang, which invades the sister chromatid. Polymerase then uses the sister chromatid as a template to fill in the sequence on the broken ends. The strands are eventually resolved to separate, resulting in complete sister chromatids. In contrast, during the rest of the cell cycle or in non-dividing cells, the cell employs the faster but less accurate process of Non-Homologous End Joining (NHEJ). The exact mechanism The processing of DNA ends during NHEJ is not fully understood and is not the same for each break; even identical breaks in the same location show variation in end processing \[[@R34]\]. Blunted DNA ends are subsequently ligated through the action of XLF:XRCC4:DNA ligase IV complex. Although the immediate threat to the cell is averted by repair of the DSB, repair by NHEJ often results in deletions or frame shifts in the repaired area as a result of end processing.
